blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Two services format Sunday 28 December 2031 with the pattern "YYYY-MM-dd". One builds its formatter with Locale.US, the other with Locale.UK. 1 January 2032 is a Thursday. What do they print?

options.text: Both print 2031-12-28, since the date falls before 1 January 2032
options.says: YYYY is the week-based year, which can differ from the calendar year in the last days of December

options.text: Both print 2032-12-28, since the week that holds 1 January belongs to 2032
options.says: which days make up that week depends on the locale: under UK rules the week starts on Monday 29 December, so the Sunday is not in it

options.text: The US one prints 2032-12-28 and the UK one 2031-12-28, since US weeks start on Sunday and UK weeks on Monday
options.says: the US week of Sunday 28 December holds 1 January, so it belongs to 2032; the UK (ISO) week holding 1 January starts on Monday 29 December

options.text: The US one prints 2031-12-28 and the UK one 2032-12-28, since UK weeks start on Monday and US weeks on Sunday
options.says: the start days are right but the outcome is reversed: under UK (ISO) rules the Sunday closes the week of 22 December, which belongs to 2031

origin.section: Pattern Letters Are Case-Sensitive, and YYYY Is the Year of the Week

questions.stem: A sign-up form validates birth dates with DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd/MM/yyyy", Locale.ROOT).withResolverStyle(ResolverStyle.STRICT) and LocalDate.parse. A user types 15/06/1990. What happens?

options.text: It is read as 15 June 1990, since STRICT refuses a date only when the calendar lacks that day
options.says: STRICT also refuses to assume an era, and yyyy is a year-of-era, so even a real date is refused

options.text: It is read as 15 June 1990, since yyyy and uuuu give the same year for every date of the current era
options.says: they print the same, but under STRICT a year-of-era without an era gives no LocalDate

options.text: It is refused, since under STRICT every year-of-era needs an era alongside it
options.says: STRICT with yyyy refuses every date; uuuu, the proleptic year, needs no era

options.text: It is refused, since under STRICT every field needs its pattern letter written in capitals
options.says: case picks the field, not the strictness: the page's STRICT uuuu-MM-dd formatter reads 2026-02-28 with lower-case letters for the year and day

origin.section: ofPattern Turns 30 February Into the 28th Unless the Resolver Is STRICT, and STRICT Needs uuuu

questions.stem: A mail service keeps `static final DateTimeFormatter LETTER = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("d MMMM uuuu", Locale.US);`. For a French customer the handler runs `LETTER.withLocale(Locale.FRANCE); return LETTER.format(date);`, while another thread formats a letter for a US customer at the same moment. Which dates do the two letters show?

options.text: Both show the month in French, since the French handler set the locale on the constant both threads share
options.says: a formatter is immutable; withLocale returns a new formatter and leaves LETTER as it was

options.text: Both show the month in English, since the French handler set the locale on a copy it never stored
options.says: withLocale returned a new formatter; the handler discarded it and formatted with the unchanged US constant

options.text: Each shows its customer's language, since each thread sees the locale its own handler set
options.says: a formatter has no per-thread state; the locale is fixed when the formatter is built

options.text: Each shows its customer's language, since LETTER.format uses the formatter that withLocale returned
options.says: LETTER still names the US formatter; the one withLocale returned was never stored, so format cannot use it

origin.section: Month and Day Names Come From a Locale, So Name One

questions.stem: An ingest service reads partner event times with LocalDateTime.parse(text, DateTimeFormatter.ISO_OFFSET_DATE_TIME) and stores the result in a column that holds UTC. A partner sends 2031-11-14T09:30:00-03:00. What is stored?

options.text: 2031-11-14T12:30, since the parsed value keeps the date and time shifted by the offset
options.says: LocalDateTime keeps only the date and time fields; nothing converts the value to UTC

options.text: 2031-11-14T09:30, since the parsed value keeps the date and time but not the offset
options.says: LocalDateTime has nowhere to keep the offset, so it is dropped without an error and the event is stored three hours early

options.text: Nothing, since parsing fails when the text holds an offset the target type can't store
options.says: parsing succeeds: the extra offset field is read and then dropped

options.text: Nothing, since ISO_OFFSET_DATE_TIME expects Z rather than a numeric offset
options.says: ISO_OFFSET_DATE_TIME reads Z and numeric offsets alike, as the page's +01:00 example shows

origin.section: An Offset in the Text Is Part of the Value, So Parse Into a Type That Keeps It

concepts: A DateTimeFormatter is immutable, so one static final instance is safe on every thread, and withLocale or withZone return a new formatter whose result must be kept.
STRICT with yyyy and no era field refuses every date, because a year-of-era needs an era STRICT won't assume; uuuu works.
